item.text: {"question_id":"5B.4","answer":"The López Obrador administration adopted some formal measures that could support participation and formalization, including USMCA continuity, a simplified tax regime for MSMEs and self-employed workers, and tax-administration tools intended to reduce compliance burdens and evasion (BATCH-0004-E017; BATCH-0014-E015; BATCH-0017-E007). However, the supplied evidence does not establish consistently fair enforcement or broad 2023 job-creation effects. World Bank indicators show 41 subnational regulations introducing a pro-competitive framework, but the sustainable industrial-park framework was not adopted and IFC nearshoring transactions remained at zero in 2023 (BATCH-0052-E016). Implementation was therefore mixed: some financial and employment-service outputs advanced, while selected investment and institutional initiatives did not proceed as planned (BATCH-0052-E016; BATCH-0052-E017). Adverse evidence is strongest in energy and major infrastructure. USTR alleged that electricity dispatch, permits, fuel standards, and gas-network access favored CFE and PEMEX over private competitors; these allegations are relevant to equal competition but remain a U.S. trade-dispute position without Mexico’s full response or final adjudication (BATCH-0046-E001; BATCH-0047-E012). The administration also pursued a 2023 reform package that would allow construction before all permits, facilitate unilateral contract termination, limit indemnities, and expand executive discretion over private concessions, although the package was proposed rather than shown here as enacted (BATCH-0011-E010). The Maya Train evidence further shows repeated authorization disputes, construction resumed without an explicit judicial order under a national-security rationale, and subsequent design changes amid unresolved technical and participation concerns (BATCH-0010-E008; BATCH-0011-E007). Overall, the record supports formal improvement alongside substantial unpredictability and uneven rule application, but leaves important gaps on property-rights enforcement, entrepreneurship, and attributable job creation.","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0004-E017","BATCH-0014-E015","BATCH-0017-E007","BATCH-0052-E016","BATCH-0052-E017"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0046-E001","BATCH-0047-E012","BATCH-0011-E010","BATCH-0010-E008","BATCH-0011-E007"],"limitations_and_gaps":["The World Bank reform evidence concerns measures adopted mainly in 2021–2022 and expected or selected 2023 results; it does not establish comprehensive fair enforcement.","The 41 subnational regulations and other World Bank indicators cover selected interventions rather than the full economy, and attribution is not solely to López Obrador.","The USTR evidence presents a U.S. government position in an unresolved dispute and does not establish final legal findings or full economic effects.","Several adverse 2023 reform measures were proposals rather than demonstrated enacted law.","The supplied record provides limited direct evidence on property-rights enforcement, entrepreneurship outcomes, and job creation attributable to federal policy.","The Maya Train evidence establishes authorization and process disputes, but not final environmental damage or the ultimate legal outcome."],"corrections_made":["Removed the repeated BATCH-0014-E015 citation and narrowed its claim to enacted formalization and compliance reforms rather than 2023 enforcement or job outcomes.","Added BATCH-0052-E016 evidence on 41 pro-competitive regulations, non-adoption of the industrial-park framework, and zero nearshoring transactions.","Added BATCH-0052-E017 only as limited implementation context for employment-service and institutional results.","Qualified the USTR evidence as an interested-party trade-dispute allegation without final adjudication.","Separated enacted reforms, proposed reforms, implementation evidence, outcomes, and authorization disputes."],"reasons_to_reopen_full_ledger":[]}
